title: In their place
hook: Hillel: don't judge your fellow until you've stood in their place (Pirkei Avot 2:4)
tomorrow: what do you do in a room where nobody is acting like a person?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shammai, the strict one, taught: receive every person with a cheerful face, because the welcome is part of the gift. A cheerful face.

Someone cuts the line, snaps at the cashier, or leaves a one-star review in all capitals, and the verdict arrives in a blink. Hillel slows that blink down. In Pirkei Avot he says: don't judge your fellow until you have reached their place. Not until you've heard their side. Until you've stood where they stand. That's the answer to yesterday's question. And the Talmud tells a story about a man who managed it, on an afternoon when it was hard to do.
screen: `THE INSTANT VERDICT.` → `DON'T JUDGE YOUR FELLOW...` → `...UNTIL YOU REACH THEIR PLACE.`

segments.voice: A man had worked for years for a landowner in the south. On the eve of Yom Kippur he asked for his wages, so he could go home to his family. Give me my pay in money. I have no money. Then in produce. I have none. Land? None. Animals? None. Cushions and blankets? None. The worker shouldered his things and went home with nothing, sad. After the holiday the landowner came to his house with the wages, and donkeys loaded with food and drink. Then he asked: when I said I had no money, what did you think? Maybe you'd bought goods cheap and your cash was tied up. And when I said no cushions? Maybe you'd vowed everything you own to the Temple. That was it, said the landowner. My vow had tied up everything, and my friends have just released me from it. Then he blessed him: as you judged me on the side of merit, may God judge you on the side of merit. Here's the teaching, named plainly. In Judaism, judging others favorably, dan l'kaf zechut, is a religious duty, taught in Pirkei Avot by Joshua ben Perachiah, a chapter before Hillel's line. Not pretending nothing happened. Tipping the scale toward the reason you can't see. And the Talmud ties it to how you hope to be judged yourself.
screen: `NO MONEY, NO LAND, NO CUSHIONS.` · `HE GUESSED THE KIND REASON.` · `JUDGED ON THE SIDE OF MERIT.` · then, large: `IN THEIR PLACE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person you judged this week. Let yourself stand, for a minute, in their place: their tiredness, their morning, the thing you can't see. Then quietly name one reason, the kindest one that could be true, and leave the verdict open.
In their place: Hillel's line in Pirkei Avot, don't judge your fellow until you've reached where they stand.
Keep this one: in their place, and the scale tipped toward merit. Four sayings in.

howItsDone: Jews study Hillel's saying in Pirkei Avot alongside Joshua ben Perachiah's teaching to judge every person on the side of merit, which is treated as a religious duty in Jewish ethics.

match.prompt: the worker and the landowner: tap the pairs.
pairs: asked for his pay before Yom Kippur
had vowed all he owned to the Temple
judge on the side of merit
don't judge until you reach their place

myth: judging favorably means pretending nothing wrong happened
the worker didn't pretend he'd been paid. he tipped the scale toward the reason he couldn't see.
in the Talmud's story, the worker's guesses turn out to be true
the landowner's goods were tied up by a vow, and he came after the holiday with the wages and more.
Hillel says don't judge anyone until you've heard their side of the story
he goes further: until you have reached their place, stood where they stand.

fork.setup: your roommate didn't do the dishes, again, and didn't answer your text. Hillel's way, what's the first move?
options: stand in her place first: what might her day have been? then talk.
judge fairly: the facts say she's careless, so tell her so.
say nothing and pretend it's fine; judging is always wrong.
fork.reveal: Hillel doesn't ban judgment; he delays it until you've reached their place. the Talmud's worker still asked for his pay. he just guessed the kind reason.

original.note: Hebrew, Pirkei Avot 2:4: don't judge your fellow until you reach his place.

trapdoor: what you thought: walk a mile in someone's shoes, a nice saying.
what it means: in Jewish ethics, judging on the side of merit is a duty, and the Talmud ties it to how you hope God will judge you.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 127b tells the worker's story right after teaching that one who judges others favorably is judged favorably; Avot 1:6 gives the duty itself.
guess: standing where someone stands before you judge them
keeping a person in their proper social rank
replacing someone at work while they're away
recall: the welcome is part of the gift

chat.says: a guy yelled at me at the desk over a 20 min wait. i wanted to yell back. still mad
options: Hillel: don't judge him till you reach his place. Guess the reason you can't see.
Fair to judge. He was rude, so the honest call is that he's a rude guy.
Just pretend it didn't happen. Hillel says never notice anyone's rudeness.
chat.meaning: Hillel delays the verdict until you've stood where they stand, and the Talmud's worker guessed the kind reason, and was right.

tie.story: The worker went home unpaid on the eve of Yom Kippur, and still guessed the kind reason. He was right.
tie.friend: Zoe can stand, for a minute, in the yelling man's place before she decides who he is.

Hillel.meaning: a sage known for patience and gentleness

Pirkei Avot.meaning: Sayings of the Fathers: a book of rabbinic teachings in the Mishnah

Yom Kippur.meaning: the Day of Atonement, a solemn Jewish fast day

dan l'kaf zechut.meaning: Hebrew: judging someone on the side of merit

Talmud.meaning: the great collection of rabbinic discussion of Jewish law and lore

Joshua ben Perachiah.meaning: an early sage in Pirkei Avot who taught judging on the side of merit

sources.ref: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (Hillel: do not judge your fellow until you reach his place)
Pirkei Avot 1:6 (Joshua ben Perachiah: judge every person on the side of merit)
Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 127b (the worker and the landowner on the eve of Yom Kippur; 'as you judged me favorably, may the Omnipresent judge you favorably')
